description.narrative:
Bangladesh’s agriculture sector, employing over 40 percent of the workforce and contributing 12.5 percent to GDP, is under severe pressure from climate change. In the coastal belt, home to 38 million people, rising salinity, tidal flooding, and cyclones are steadily eroding the viability of open-field farming. By 2050, the World Bank estimates that up to one-third of the country’s agricultural GDP could be lost. While adaptive interventions such as saline-tolerant crops have shown promise, they remain vulnerable to sudden weather shocks and pests, leaving smallholders with unstable incomes and food insecurity. Protected horticulture offers a proven pathway to resilience. Low-cost polyhouses shield crops from climate stress, enable year- round cultivation, and allow farmers to achieve higher yields and profitability. Yet adoption in Bangladesh remains limited to fewer than 2,000 active units, with less than five percent penetration in coastal areas where the need is greatest. High upfront investment costs, limited access to finance, weak technical knowledge, and fragile market linkages continue to constrain uptake.
The slow uptake of protected horticulture is driven by several structural barriers. Farmers face high upfront investment costs and limited access to affordable finance, which prevents smallholders from purchasing polyhouse structures or high-value seeds. Technical knowledge of controlled farming is low, and the availability of suitable construction materials and inputs remains limited. Even when production is successful, weak value chains mean that farmers struggle to access institutional buyers or receive fair prices. At the business level, companies offering construction services and inputs, such as Agro1 and ACI, remain small in scale and face challenges in demand creation and developing viable private-sector engagement models.
The Government of Bangladesh has recognized the potential of greenhouse and protected cultivation within its climate-smart agriculture agenda. Research institutions such as the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) and the Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI) have piloted demonstration plots and training programs. Early private-sector entrants are supplying polyhouse materials and seeds, while international firms like East West Seeds and Rijk Zwaan are beginning to introduce high-value and saline-tolerant varieties. Despite these positive signs, public–private collaboration remains fragmented and insufficient to achieve scale in coastal regions. At the same time, national strategies such as the National Adaptation Plan, the Mujib Climate Prosperity Plan, and the Eighth Five-Year Plan call for expanded technology transfer, private-sector engagement, and sustainable agri-business models—providing a strong policy framework for advancing protected horticulture.

The overarching objective of this initiative is to contribute to climate-resilient and market-driven horticulture systems in coastal Bangladesh, thereby increase income and ensuring sustainable livelihoods for smallholder farmers in saline-affected regions. By piloting low-cost protected cultivation models, the project seeks to demonstrate how farmers can overcome climate-related production risks and achieve consistent returns from high-value crops.

The project will directly engage 11 farmers and nursery operators (At least 40 percent of direct beneficiaries will be women) in the coastal belt of Bangladesh. These include 5 smallholder farmers (average land size 4,360 sq. ft each), 3 medium-scale farmers (average land size 8,720 sq. ft each), and 3 nursery owners (average land size 8,720 sq. ft each).
Indirectly, the project is expected to reach approximately 200 people, including farming households, labourers employed in nurseries and polyhouses, and community members who benefit from increased availability of high-value vegetables in local markets. Youth will be engaged as workers, service providers, or entrepreneurs in input supply and marketing functions, broadening employment opportunities beyond farming alone.
